topic: Machine Learning: Classification vs Regression Scenarios

questions.scenario: A fintech enterprise is building a credit card limit assignment system. 85% of existing customers fall into lower credit limits (< $2,000), while a small tail of high-net-worth applicants requires continuous predictions up to $100,000. The data science team initially framed this as a unified regression problem using Mean Squared Error (MSE). However, the model consistently severe-underpredicts high-value limits due to extreme right-skewness and the dominance of low-value modes in gradient updates.
questions.question: Which framing shift optimally resolves the prediction bias across both common low-value modes and rare continuous high-value tails?
options: A) Reformulate the architecture into a two-stage hybrid pipeline: a binary classification model (High vs. Low Limit) followed by a specialized log-transformed regression model for the high-value segment.
B) Apply Huber Loss on the unified regression model to enforce quadratic penalties on small errors and ignore large extreme tail errors.
C) Convert the regression task into a multi-class classification problem using 10,000 uniform categorical bins of $10 increments trained via Cross-Entropy Loss.
D) Apply SMOTE-R to oversample high-value records and retain standard Mean Squared Error loss on scaled inputs without changing the target representation.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Reformulate the architecture into a two-stage hybrid pipeline: a binary classification model (High vs. Low Limit) followed by a specialized log-transformed regression model for the high-value segment.
questions.explanation: Extremely skewed target distributions with dense point-masses (e.g., $2,000) cause single-stage MSE regression models to collapse towards the majority mode. Disentangling the task into a discrete Classification stage (gating decision) and a log-transformed Regression stage (for continuous tail estimation) isolates high variance and prevents MSE gradients from being dominated by zero/low-value mode density.

questions.scenario: An IoT healthcare provider streams 128-channel EEG continuous signals (high-dimensional, 500 Hz sampling rate) to detect focal epileptic seizure onset within 100 milliseconds. The engineering team deployed a Support Vector Regression (SVR) model with a non-linear Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel to output a continuous 'Seizure Severity Score' (0.0 to 1.0). In production on edge devices, computing the kernel matrix against thousands of support vectors causes inference latency to hit 450 ms per window, breaching safety bounds.
questions.question: How should the engineering team re-architect the ML task and model selection to satisfy strict edge latency bounds (<100ms) without sacrificing sensitivity?
options: A) Re-frame the task as binary classification using Logistic Regression with L1 regularization (Lasso) on extracted spectral domain features.
B) Replace SVR with a k-Nearest Neighbors Regression (k-NN, k=1) to instantly lookup raw signal similarity without kernel transformations.
C) Retain the non-linear SVR model but increase the penalty parameter C and RBF gamma hyperparameter to force a sparser decision space.
D) Keep the SVR pipeline but downsample the streaming signal from 500 Hz to 10 Hz without applying anti-aliasing low-pass filtering.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Re-frame the task as binary classification using Logistic Regression with L1 regularization (Lasso) on extracted spectral domain features.
questions.explanation: Non-linear kernel SVR requires $O(N_{sv} \cdot d)$ inner product calculations per sample at test time, where $N_{sv}$ can be huge in high-dimensional continuous streaming. Re-framing the problem to binary classification allows using linear models like Logistic Regression with L1 regularization. L1 zeros out irrelevant feature weights, turning real-time prediction into a simple, ultra-fast sparse vector dot-product $O(d_{sparse})$, executed well under 100ms.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce platform wants to optimize customer retention. They deployed a continuous regression model predicting 'Days Until Churn' optimized with Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Business ops discovered that overestimating churn time (e.g., predicting 30 days remaining when true value is 3 days) leads to lost intervention windows and high revenue loss. Conversely, underestimating churn time (predicting 3 days when true value is 30) causes negligible loss due to a low-cost automated email campaign.
questions.question: Why is the current framing failing business objectives, and what is the mathematically sound remedy?
options: A) Symmetric regression loss functions like MAE penalize over-prediction and under-prediction identically; the task should be re-framed into discrete probabilistic risk buckets with cost-sensitive decision thresholds.
B) MAE is overly sensitive to outliers; replacing it with Mean Squared Error (RMSE) naturally imposes non-symmetric penalties favoring under-predictions.
C) Continuous target values are non-stationary; applying Z-score normalization directly to the target variable eliminates asymmetric operational costs.
D) The model must switch from supervised regression to unsupervised K-Means clustering to discover natural unlabelled churn cohorts without loss functions.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Symmetric regression loss functions like MAE penalize over-prediction and under-prediction identically; the task should be re-framed into discrete probabilistic risk buckets with cost-sensitive decision thresholds.
questions.explanation: Standard regression loss functions (MAE/MSE) assume symmetric penalty structures ($L(y, \hat{y}) = L(\hat{y}, y)$). When business costs of error are heavily asymmetric (False Negatives >> False Positives), framing the task as probabilistic classification (e.g., 'Will Churn in <7 days?') permits applying Custom Cost Matrices or adjusting class decision thresholds (Bayes Risk Minimization) to align model outputs with operational financial risk.
